newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN split over timing of Burma's entry - Alatas.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN split over timing of Burma's entry - Alatas.

text.p: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) wants Burma to become a full member but is split over when it should happen, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said on Monday.
"There is a view among some ASEAN members as to the timing, the best time when Myanmar (Burma) should enter, not on the principle of Myanmar's entry into ASEAN," Alatas said.
"As to the entry of Burma, or the acceptance of Burma as the 10th member of ASEAN, there is no split whatsoever and there has never been any disagreement among ASEAN," Alatas said.

Speaking to reporters after a meeting between visiting Indonesia President Suharto and Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, Alatas said Burma has to first meet "technical procedures" for joining the seven-member grouping.
Key among these is Rangoon's ability to participate in the ASEAN Free Trade Area, which is scheduled to become fully operational over the next seven years, he said.
Alatas stressed that Rangoon's human rights record would never be a factor in its membership.

"We are not talking about the internal situtation of Myanmar, because no single organisation in the world, including the United Nations, makes it as a criterion or requirement (for membership), the internal situation of a country," Alatas said.
"So why should ASEAN adopt a rule that nowhere else is applied?"
ASEAN, comprising Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, groups some of the fastest growing economies in the world.
Next year, Cambodia and Laos are slated to become full members.
Rangoon, whose military regime has been roundly denounced in the West for its repression of Aung San Suu Kyi's pro-democracy movement, has formally applied to become the group's 10th member.
Reforming the junta stands a better chance of working if Rangoon is constantly engaged in regional dialogues and meetings instead of being hit with sanctions, officials say.
Philippine President Fidel Ramos said last week that ASEAN might review its policy of "constructive engagement" towards Burma at an ASEAN summit in November.
Ramos said the consensus among ASEAN foreign ministers remained that the group may eventually admit Burma as a member provided it made progress on trade and political reforms.
ASEAN says its policy of "constructive engagement" is aimed at keeping Burma from becoming isolated.
